slides.title: Chapter 10: Jacobi Fields
slides.notes: This chapter is where curvature finally becomes visible as the behavior of nearby geodesics. The single equation we build today controls focusing, the failure of minimization, and the global shape of the cut locus. Tell students to keep one mental picture throughout: a one-parameter family of geodesics, and the variation field that records how they drift apart. Everything else is the linearization of the geodesic equation around one geodesic.

slides.title: Geodesic Variations and Variation Fields
slides.notes: Start concretely: a variation is a sheet of geodesics, and the variation field is the velocity of that sheet in the transverse direction. Stress that the symmetry lemma exchanging the two covariant derivatives is the only tool that turns the geodesic condition into a clean equation for J. Draw the arrows yourself on the board so students see J as living along a single fixed geodesic. The whole chapter is the study of which fields J can arise this way.

slides.title: The Jacobi Equation
slides.notes: This is the heart of the chapter, so derive it slowly: it is just the geodesic equation differentiated transversally, with the Riemann tensor measuring the failure of second derivatives to commute. Emphasize that it is a genuine linear ODE, so existence and uniqueness give a 2n-dimensional solution space parameterized by initial value and initial covariant derivative. Point out the sign intuition immediately: positive curvature is restoring, negative curvature is repelling. Note the two tangential Jacobi fields so students can always quotient them out and focus on normal fields.

slides.title: Jacobi Fields in Constant Curvature
slides.notes: This is the slide students remember: three curvature signs, three growth laws. Show how the vector equation collapses to the scalar ODE f double-prime plus k f equals zero once you align J with a parallel normal frame. The positive case oscillates and so it returns to zero, producing the first conjugate point on the sphere at distance pi over root k. Emphasize that flat and negative curvature give monotone growth, so geodesics never refocus there, which is the analytic seed of the Cartan-Hadamard picture.

slides.title: Conjugate Points
slides.notes: Define conjugate points twice: once as a Jacobi field vanishing at both ends, and once as a singularity of the differential of the exponential map. Make the equivalence explicit because students often hold only one of these and miss that they are the same statement. The sphere is the canonical example, where every great circle refocuses at the antipode with high multiplicity. Foreshadow the next slide: a conjugate point is precisely where a geodesic stops being a local minimum of length.

slides.title: The Second Variation of Energy
slides.notes: Frame this as computing the Hessian of the energy functional at a geodesic. The first variation vanishing is exactly the geodesic equation; the second variation is where curvature decides stability. Show the integration by parts so students see the Jacobi operator emerge as the kernel of this quadratic form, tying the analysis back to slide three. Emphasize the sign: positive sectional curvature can make the second variation negative, which is the analytic reason great circles past the antipode no longer minimize.

slides.title: The Index Form and the Index Lemma
slides.notes: Introduce the index form as the polarization of the second variation, so its diagonal is what we computed before. The Index Lemma is the workhorse: with no conjugate point inside, Jacobi fields minimize against all competitors sharing the same endpoints, which underlies most comparison theorems. Then state the converse intuition: each conjugate point passed contributes a negative direction, so the index counts them with multiplicity. Mention Morse theory lightly to motivate why this counting matters for the topology of path spaces.

slides.title: Cut Points and the Cut Locus
slides.notes: Distinguish carefully between conjugate points, a local first-order phenomenon, and cut points, a global minimization phenomenon. The cut point is whichever comes first: a conjugate point or the arrival of a competing minimizer of equal length. Use the sphere where both coincide at the antipode, then contrast with a flat torus where the cut locus is entirely from competing geodesics with no conjugate points at all. Conclude that the injectivity domain of the exponential map is the star-shaped region bounded by the cut locus, which is the natural chart for global geometry.

slides.title: Locally Symmetric Spaces: nabla R = 0
slides.notes: Present locally symmetric spaces as the place where everything from this chapter becomes computable. With parallel curvature the Riemann operator is constant in a parallel frame, so the Jacobi equation becomes a constant-coefficient linear system. Diagonalizing the curvature operator splits it into scalar oscillators, recovering the sin and sinh behavior from slide four in each eigendirection. Emphasize that this is why symmetric spaces are the standard testbeds: conjugate points and the cut locus are read straight off the eigenvalues.

slides.title: What Jacobi Fields Buy Us
slides.notes: Close by collapsing the chapter to three ideas: one linear equation, the focusing it predicts, and the minimization it controls. Ask students to run the diagnostic out loud for the sphere, the plane, and hyperbolic space so the sin, linear, and sinh trichotomy is automatic. Remind them that conjugate points are local and first-order while cut points are global, and that locally symmetric spaces make all of it explicit. This sets up the comparison theorems that use these tools to convert curvature bounds into statements about distance, volume, and topology.
